analysis.one_liner: Bars credit card rate hikes on old balances without notice, penalty fees for on-time payers, and over-limit fees.
analysis.headline: Senator Dodd's bill to restrict credit card penalty rates and fees died in the Senate Banking Committee with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required credit card companies to give 15 days' notice before raising someone's interest rate and let the customer cancel and pay off the old balance at the old rate. It banned charging penalty fees to people who paid on time or in full, banned over-limit fees on purchases the company itself approved, forced clearer disclosures about teaser rates and how long paying the minimum really takes, restricted credit cards for people under 21, and let bankruptcy courts treat debts carrying extremely high interest rates more leniently.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card holders, especially the tens of millions who carry a balance and get hit with penalty rates, over-limit fees, and retroactive interest increases on money they already owed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Credit card customers who carry balances

how_it_helps.text: Card companies would have to give at least 15 days' advance notice before raising an interest rate, and could not apply a higher rate to balances already owed; a customer who canceled could pay off the old balance at the old rate [S3][S2].

No finance charge could be imposed on amounts paid on time, no fee or penalty for paying in full or paying more than the minimum, and no over-limit fee on transactions the creditor approved in advance [S3][S2].

Card offers would have to clearly disclose the permanent rate that applies after a teaser rate ends, plus the conditions that could void the teaser rate; statements would have to show how many months and how much total cost paying only the minimums involves, and disclose late-fee deadlines and postmark cutoffs [S3].

Lenders could not issue cards to anyone under 21 without a co-signer, proof of independent ability to repay, or completion of approved credit counseling, and the same rules would cover student affinity cards marketed through colleges [S3].

In bankruptcy, credit card debts carrying an interest rate more than 20 percentage points above the prime rate would not count toward the legal presumptions that make discharge harder, giving debtors a remedy against abusive rates [S3][S2].
Penalties for lender violations of open-end credit rules would double, with a $500 minimum and higher amounts for a pattern of violations [S3][S2].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers and banks, which would lose revenue from penalty interest rates applied to existing balances, over-limit fees, fees charged to on-time payers, and campus affinity-card marketing to students.

drawbacks.text: Card issuers argued in this era that restricting penalty pricing and fees would raise costs for all borrowers and tighten access to credit for riskier customers; a restriction on their ability to reprice risk shifts losses onto other cardholders and people who may no longer qualify.

The bankruptcy provision lets courts discharge debts run up at rates more than 20 points above prime, which increases lender losses that could be recovered through higher prices for other customers [S3].
The under-21 rules would make it harder for young adults to build an independent credit history without a co-signer or a counseling course [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are targeted and real: notice before rate hikes, no punishing people for paying on time, honest disclosure about teaser rates and minimum-payment traps, and guardrails for student marketing. The main costs fall on the card industry's fee and penalty-rate revenue, though some of that cost can be passed through to borrowers as higher standard rates or reduced credit access. On balance the benefits to cardholders carrying balances outweigh the drawbacks, which is why versions of most of these ideas eventually became federal law in a later Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there with zero cosponsors and no hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Senator Dodd, the senior Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, introduced the Credit CARD Act of 2004 on July 22, 2004 [S1][S5].
The bill was referred the same day to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, on which Dodd served [S5][S3].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].

The bill's core ideas — advance notice of rate increases, no fees for on-time payments, no over-limit fees on approved transactions, clearer teaser-rate and payoff disclosures — went unenacted in that Congress [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers came out ahead: they kept charging penalty rates on existing balances, over-limit fees, and fees to on-time payers through the end of the Congress, with no recorded vote ever taken. Cardholders paying those fees paid on.

for.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-CT), senior member of the Senate Banking Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its companion protections on the Senate floor and referred it to the Banking Committee, where he served.

against.name: Richard Shelby
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; the committee never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: Credit card issuers and banks
against.role: Card industry facing restrictions on penalty rates and fees
against.what_they_did: Opposed credit card pricing and fee restrictions in this era and supported instead the industry-backed bankruptcy legislation moving through the same Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded and no senator cosponsored the bill, so its support never took measurable shape; it was introduced by a Democrat into a committee run by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would directly cut into the industry's most profitable practices: raising rates on existing balances, penalizing on-time payers, charging over-limit fees on transactions the issuer itself approved, and marketing cards to students. Those revenues come straight out of cardholders' pockets, so the industry's interest ran against customers' in this bill.
The bill bars issuing cards to under-21 students through college affinity agreements unless a co-signer, proof of repayment ability, or counseling is provided, curbing campus-based card marketing.
The bill creates a Board approval pathway for nonprofits to qualify under the under-21 counseling requirement, with conflict-of-interest standards, giving qualified agencies a defined role.
